summary:
Scotland is a constituent nation of the United Kingdom. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to the Scottish Parliament, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at United Kingdom level; the findings below are those specific to Scotland.

Trans people in Scotland change their legal gender under the United Kingdom Gender Recognition Act 2004. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced to the Scottish Parliament in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only to Scotland. The United Kingdom government blocked the Bill under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while it awaited royal assent, the first time that power has been used to overturn Scottish legislation, so the reformed procedure the Scottish Parliament legislated for is not in force in Scotland.

Hate crime in Scotland is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed by the Scottish Parliament in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and brought into force on 1 April 2024. It lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier Scottish legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service publication 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, according to the Scottish Government report published 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 Act. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent of recorded hate crimes carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category.

Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving the removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, in both custody and stop-and-search contexts. Where a person's lived gender differs from their sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The case was heard in February 2026, when the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant was challenging a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform such marriages.
tangentialFactors:
The two hate-crime series measure different things over different periods. The COPFS figures count charges decided by the prosecution service in 2025-26; the Scottish Government figures count crimes recorded by the police in 2024-25. Both are raw counts, and only the police report supplies a population denominator, and then only for total hate crime.

Within the 2025-26 charge totals, transgender-identity aggravation at 104 charges stands well below sexual-orientation aggravation at 2,062. The categories are not interchangeable and the gap reflects both the number of charges brought and the population each protects, so it cannot be read as a measure of relative danger to a trans visitor.

The section 35 block on the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was the first use of that power against Scottish legislation, establishing that United Kingdom government review can stop Scottish gender-recognition reform before it takes effect. The inventory does not record whether the Bill has been reintroduced, litigated or otherwise revived.

Hate-crime charging in Scotland is rising overall: 7,115 charges in 2025-26 is the highest total since 2003-04, an increase that spans all protected characteristics rather than the transgender-identity category alone, which rose from 86 to 104 charges in one year.
localsOnly:
Scottish residents obtained no new legal-gender pathway from the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill, which was passed by the Scottish Parliament in December 2022 and stopped before royal assent under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998.

Prosecution of hate crime in Scotland is carried out by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, which reported 104 transgender-identity aggravation charges for 2025-26, up 21% year on year and the highest since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 came into force on 1 April 2024. The 2009 penalty-enhancement provision for gender-identity-motivated offending also applies in Scottish courts.

Custody and search practice for residents is set locally: Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 places searches removing more than outer layers on a biological-sex basis in custody and stop-and-search, with an officer of the person's lived gender provided on request where practicable, and the Scottish Prison Service's trans-custody guidance was struck down by the Court of Session on 19 June 2026 as lacking a lawful basis for sex segregation.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been available in Scotland since 16 December 2014, and religious bodies and celebrants may decline to solemnise such ceremonies without obligation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Scottish Government's 2018 announcement of an 'X' sex descriptor on identity documents and a minimum transition age of 16 is recorded as an announcement; the inventory does not record whether either was implemented, so the current availability of an 'X' marker on Scottish residents' documents remains unresolved.

Whether the Scottish Prison Service reissued trans-custody guidance after the Court of Session judgment of 19 June 2026, and whether that judgment has been appealed, are not sourced here.

The hate-crime figures are charges brought and crimes recorded, not convictions and not a measure of victimisation prevalence. No per-capita rate exists in this inventory for the transgender-identity category, only the raw count of 104 charges for 2025-26.

No trans-specific violence or mortality figure for Scotland appears in this inventory; nothing on that question can be sourced from it.

Several instruments that affect trans travellers across Great Britain rather than in Scotland alone are carried at United Kingdom level in the parent record: the British Transport Police strip-searching policy amended in April 2025, the Equality and Human Rights Commission single-sex spaces guidance in force from August 2026, and the NHS England ward and prescribing rules for England.
